analysis.one_liner: Tightens railroad work-hour limits, protects workers who report safety problems, and sets passenger safety standards.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1999 with one cosponsor, the bill sat in a House Transportation subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal railroad safety laws for 1999 through 2002. It would limit how many hours railroad workers can be kept on duty, require railroads to write fatigue-management plans, give workers new legal protection when they report injuries or refuse unsafe work, require stronger passenger car escape windows and locomotive fuel tanks, and fund 400 additional federal safety inspectors through fees on the railroads. It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Ground Transportation Subcommittee, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Railroad workers first: the bill would cap duty hours across multiple employers and contractors, require separate quiet sleeping quarters, protect workers from being fired or disciplined for reporting injuries, cooperating with investigations, reporting hazardous conditions, or refusing to work in imminent danger, and add civil and criminal penalties for harassment or interference with safety investigations. Rail passengers would get escape windows and doors on cars, tougher fuel tanks and corner posts on locomotives, and a deadline for positive train control on busy passenger and hazmat corridors. The public would also get toll-free hotlines to report grade-crossing signal failures.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's own findings state that employee fatigue remains a critical problem and that harassment and intimidation of railroad employees cast doubt on the reliability of rail safety statistics [S3].

It would count all time worked for any railroad carrier or independent contractor toward hours-of-service limits, close loopholes around workers holding two railroad jobs, and require eight hours' notice and guaranteed days off for crews driven to work sites [S2] [S3].

It would bar railroads from threatening, intimidating, disciplining, or firing employees for reporting a work-related injury, cooperating with a safety investigation, furnishing accident facts, reporting a hazardous condition, or refusing to work in the face of imminent danger — with reinstatement, back pay, and punitive damages for violations [S2] [S3].

It would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to two years in prison, to obstruct a railroad safety investigation or intimidate witnesses, and would require an annual independent audit of each railroad's accident-reporting process [S2] [S3].

After January 1, 2002, passenger cars would need emergency windows and quick-release doors; new passenger locomotives would need internal, compartmentalized fuel tanks; and the Transportation Secretary would have to require positive train control — technology that automatically stops trains — on high-priority corridors by 2003 [S2] [S3].
Fees on railroad carriers would fund 400 additional federal railroad safety inspectors, and workers would get a right to separate, quiet sleeping quarters free from switching-yard noise [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Railroad carriers and the contractors that work for them. They would bear the cost of rewriting schedules and staffing around the work-hour limits, building fatigue-management plans, upgrading sleeping quarters, installing positive train control and new passenger-car equipment, paying fees to fund 400 more inspectors, and facing new civil and criminal penalties. Managers personally face a new exclusion-from-employment penalty for harassing workers over injury reporting.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly: railroads would fund 400 extra inspectors through fees, install positive train control on high-priority corridors within a few years, retrofit passenger cars with emergency windows and crashworthy corner posts, and rework crew scheduling and lodging [S2] [S3].

The bill creates an exception for dually employed workers: a railroad is not responsible for an hours-of-service violation caused by a worker's schedule at another employer if none of its managers had actual knowledge of it, which good-faith critics could call a loophole even though it requires annual written notice rules [S2] [S3].

Rules proposed unanimously by the industry-led Railroad Safety Advisory Committee would go forward without any cost-benefit analysis or outside agency review, a fast track that favors consensus over scrutiny [S3].
The bill leans heavily on paperwork — fatigue plans, audits, quarterly reports — that regulators would need to review and enforce for the promised safety gains to materialize [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains target documented problems — the bill's own findings concede that employee fatalities and derailments had not fallen while fatigue and intimidation persisted [S3]. The costs fall on a concentrated industry, and some provisions (like the dual-employment knowledge carve-out and the no-cost-benefit fast track for committee-consensus rules) soften the bill's edge. But the core trade — enforceable rest limits and real whistleblower protection in exchange for industry compliance spending — favors workers and passengers.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, was passed along to the Ground Transportation Subcommittee two days later, and never came back out — no markup, no floor vote, nothing — before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ronnie Shows introduced the bill on July 30, 1999, with Rep. Nick Lampson joining as the only cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and on August 2 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Ground Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote, never reached the House floor, and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroad carriers and their contractors were better off: they avoided the compliance costs, inspection fees, certification requirements, and new liability the bill would have imposed. Railroad workers and passengers gained nothing, since the safety and whistleblower provisions never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only two Democrats sponsoring the bill and no votes or floor activity, so the partisan shape of any opposition cannot be determined from the sources.

industries.note: The bill would cap and count all duty hours across employers and contractors, mandate fatigue plans and quiet sleeping quarters, require annual accident-reporting audits, fund 400 more federal inspectors through carrier fees, and expose carriers and their managers to civil and criminal penalties for intimidating injured workers or obstructing investigations. Carriers' interest in weaker rest rules and less record-keeping runs against worker and passenger safety.

industries.industry: Railroad contractors and subcontractors (signal, dispatch, maintenance, crew transport)
industries.note: Contractor employees would be brought under hours-of-service limits, contractor duty time would count toward limits, and carriers would be held responsible for contractors' scheduling practices — raising contractor labor costs and tightening carrier oversight of them.

New emergency windows, crashworthy corner posts, and compartmentalized fuel tanks would force redesign and retooling of passenger equipment, a compliance cost, but the standards would apply across the market and drive orders for updated equipment.
